extracted.intended_audience: inventors and patent attorneys prosecuting software, fintech, AI/ML, diagnostics, and business-method patents in the United States
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and legal guidance on applying the Mayo/Alice two-step framework to determine U.S. patent eligibility, with examples, USPTO examination guidance, and concrete claim-drafting and prosecution strategies to survive §101 challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-step test (Mayo/Alice framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-step inquiry used to determine whether a claimed invention is directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 1: Determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon. If not, the claim is patent-eligible and analysis ends. If yes, proceed to Step 2. Step 2: Determine whether the claim includes an 'inventive concept' — elements individually or in combination that transform the judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter (must be 'significantly more').

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: The court or examiner first determines whether the claims are directed to one of the judicially recognized exceptions to patentability: abstract ideas, laws of nature, or natural phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is not directed to a judicial exception, it is patent-eligible and the inquiry ends. If it is, proceed to the inventive-concept inquiry. Courts evaluate this on a claim-by-claim basis; look to claim focus and the problem the claim addresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2 — Inventive concept requirement ('significantly more')
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claim is directed to an abstract idea, it may be patent-eligible if it contains elements (alone or ordered combination) that constitute an inventive concept sufficient to transform the abstract idea into an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventive concept cannot be satisfied by mere recitation of generic computer components, conventional steps, or well-understood activity. The inventive concept can be a specific technical improvement, unconventional combination, solution to a technical problem, or non-generic implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO abstract-idea category: Mathematical concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical formulas, equations, calculations, geometric relationships; algorithms for data compression, encryption, statistical analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that are essentially mathematical concepts are likely to be characterized as abstract ideas at Step 1 unless integrated into a practical application that improves technology or produces a technical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO abstract-idea category: Certain methods of organizing human activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental economic practices, commercial interactions, managing personal behavior, legal obligations (e.g., hedging risk, intermediated settlement, advertising methods, contractual relationships).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business-method-type claims often fall into this category and are vulnerable under Step 1 unless tied to a specific technological implementation that meaningfully integrates the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO abstract-idea category: Mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts performed in the human mind, including observation, evaluation, judgment, and opinion (e.g., comparing data, categorizing information, forming a diagnosis based on observed symptoms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that can be performed mentally or with pen and paper are likely abstract ideas; to survive, the claim should show a technological application or specific machine implementation that adds 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: What does NOT constitute an inventive concept (negative indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of claim features that courts and examiners have held are insufficient to supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: generic computer implementation (performing the idea on a generic computer); conventional steps or routine processes; mere 'apply it on a computer' language; field-of-use limitations without more; insignificant extra-solution activity such as routine data gathering or post-solution activity. Example: 'a method of hedging risk using a computer' fails because the computer is merely a tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific technical improvements (positive inventive-concept indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimed features that improve computer functionality, network performance, data security, or system efficiency are strong evidence of an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize how the invention changes the way computers operate or solves a computer-technology-specific problem (e.g., reduced latency via dynamic partitioning of queries). Case example: Enfish (self-referential database improved computer functionality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconventional combinations (positive inventive-concept indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arranging known elements in a new way that produces unexpected results may constitute an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if individual elements are known, emphasize the ordered combination and explain how the arrangement produces benefits prior systems could not achieve. Provide specification support and, if possible, evidence of unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that solve a technical problem (positive inventive-concept indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim features specifically tailored to address a technological challenge (e.g., preserving website look-and-feel while displaying third-party content) support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie claim language to the technical problem solved rather than the business objective. DDR Holdings is an example where the claimed solution was 'necessarily rooted in computer technology' and thus patent-eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-generic implementations and particular machines/tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations reciting particular machines, hardware structures, or non-generic implementations that go beyond general-purpose computing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that name specific machine architectures, sensor arrangements, protocols, or transformations are harder to dismiss as merely implementing an abstract idea on generic hardware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software and computer-implemented inventions: focus on technical contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Software patents face steep scrutiny; claims that simply automate manual processes, organize data, or perform calculations on generic hardware are highly vulnerable under Alice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To survive, software claims should be drafted to claim improvements in computer functionality (memory management, processing speed, security, novel user interfaces) and include technical detail in the claim and specification. Enfish and McRO illustrate software wins when technical improvements are claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business methods and fintech: typically vulnerable
rubrics_metrics.description: Business method patents (pricing, transactions, account management, etc.) are frequently rejected as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business-method claims generally must be tied to a specific technological implementation that solves a technical problem to survive. Purely economic practice claims are unlikely to be allowable after Alice and Bilski.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic methods and medical technology: Mayo overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that simply observe natural phenomena and make diagnoses are susceptible under the Mayo/Alice framework (laws of nature/natural phenomena).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrating inventive concept often requires showing that claimed steps add a novel application or transformation beyond routine observation/analysis; Mayo invalidated claims that were only conventional steps around a natural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI and machine-learning patents: show technical improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to training models, classifying data, or making predictions are often characterized as abstract mathematical algorithms unless they improve a particular technical process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to show how the AI/ML system improves system performance, resource utilization, accuracy in a technical context, or otherwise addresses a concrete technical problem; avoid claiming general-purpose model training or abstract data analysis alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: What still gets through Alice scrutiny (physical transformation/hardware focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions involving physical transformation, specific hardware improvements, or manufacturing processes are generally less affected by Alice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical devices, chemical compositions, novel medical devices with structural innovations, and manufacturing/process inventions remain subject primarily to novelty/non-obviousness analysis rather than §101 hurdles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy — Frame the invention as a technical improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting claims, present the invention as solving a specific technical problem or improving technology rather than as a business outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use claim language and specification examples that articulate the technical problem, the technical solution, and measurable technical benefits (e.g., reduced latency, improved throughput). Good vs bad claim examples are provided in the guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy — Include specific technical limitations in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid generic terms; specify architectures, memory structures, data flows, protocols, or other technical details in claim limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more concrete and specific the limitations (rather than 'a processor' or 'a network'), the less likely an examiner or court will treat the claim as a mere abstract idea executed on generic hardware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy — Demonstrate unconventional combinations in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize how claimed element combinations are non-routine and deliver unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide disclosure explaining why the combination is different from prior art, how it works, and why it achieves results prior systems could not; support arguments with examples, test data, or declarations where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy — Tie abstract concepts to physical components
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate abstract data-processing or analysis steps with concrete sensors, devices, outputs, or other physical components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linking an algorithm to a specific sensor arrangement or physical output can help transform an abstract idea into a practical application under USPTO guidance and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy — Use dependent claims to add implementation detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft narrower dependent claims that recite specific implementations, architectures, or parameters to preserve protection if broader independent claims are vulnerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims can survive even when broader claims are invalidated; include multiple tiers of specificity in the filing to maximize value and fallback positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy — Build a strong specification supporting technical achievements
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should explain the technical problem, prior shortcomings, how the invention solves the problem, and any unexpected results or performance improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners and courts look to the specification to assess whether claim elements are conventional. Provide concrete examples, implementation details, test results, and explanation of how the claimed features produce technical benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO 2019 Revised Guidance — Step 2A Prong One (recitation of judicial exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the USPTO's 2019 guidance, the examiner first determines whether the claim recites a judicial exception (abstract idea/law/natural phenomenon) using the enumerated groupings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim does not fall into the enumerated categories, the examiner should not make a §101 rejection. This step formalizes Step 1 and emphasizes use of the USPTO's groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO 2019 Revised Guidance — Step 2A Prong Two (practical application/integration)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim recites a judicial exception, the examiner evaluates whether the additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical application examples include improvements to computer or technology functionality, application with a particular machine, transformation of an article to a different state, or other meaningful limitations beyond linking the exception to a technological environment. If integrated, the claim is patent-eligible and analysis ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO 2019 Revised Guidance — Step 2B (inventive concept evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application under Step 2A, the examiner considers whether additional claim elements amount to 'significantly more' than the exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must assess whether the additional elements are well-understood, routine, and conventional; after Berkheimer, factual support is required for assertions of conventionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner burden after Berkheimer (factual support requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Berkheimer v. HP, an examiner asserting that claim elements are conventional must provide factual support (references, affidavits, or official notice) rather than conclusory assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants can challenge unsupported examiner assertions and demand factual evidence. Use declarations or technical evidence to show non-conventionality where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective responses to a §101/Alice rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactics to overcome examiner rejections under §101/Alice during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include arguing the claim is not directed to an abstract idea (show it's a specific technological improvement), demonstrating practical application (integration into a machine or transformation), showing unconventional elements with evidence (declarations, prior-art distinctions), amending claims to add technical limitations, and challenging the examiner to meet their burden on conventionality per Berkheimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and limits of §101 invalidation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is invalidated under §101, that claim is unenforceable; widespread invalidation can render an entire patent worthless and often cannot be cured by amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because §101 invalidity attacks the fundamental concept, narrower claim amendment may not salvage eligibility. This underscores the importance of claiming technical contributions and building a strong specification at the drafting stage.
